How Tide Pools Survive the Winter

By Maya Okafor · January 12, 2026

Every January, the rocky shelf below Point Reyes becomes one of the harshest places on the coast. Storm swells scour the rocks, freshwater from the hills lowers the salinity, and night-time low tides expose the pools to air that can drop below freezing. Yet when spring comes, the same anemones and sculpins are still there.

Researchers at the Bodega Marine Lab have spent a decade tracking how these small communities hold on. Their findings, published this month, suggest that shelter matters more than temperature tolerance.

Three strategies

The team identified three broad strategies that resident species use:

  • Retreat into crevices
    • Sculpins wedge themselves under ledges
    • Hermit crabs cluster in the deepest pools
  • Close up and wait: anemones retract their tentacles for days at a time
  • Grow slowly: coralline algae nearly stop growing between December and March

Not every species manages. The study recorded steep losses among purple urchins in years with prolonged rain.

We expected cold to be the killer. It turned out that fresh water was far more dangerous for most animals.

Okafor notes that the sampling sites were chosen in 2016, before the marine heatwave, so the baseline already reflects a stressed system.

  1. Sample monthly at the lowest tide.
  2. Count every animal larger than 5 mm.
  3. Log salinity and water temperature.

The full dataset is available from the lab's open data page.
